questions.stem: A student heats a white solid and records that it melts over a range of 98-104°C. What does this suggest about the substance?

options.text: It is a pure substance with a melting point of 101°C
It is a mixture, because pure substances have sharp melting points
The thermometer is faulty
It is a compound that decomposes on heating

questions.explanation: Pure substances have a sharp, fixed melting point. If a substance melts over a range of temperatures, it indicates that it is impure (a mixture). Impurities lower the melting point and broaden the melting range. A pure substance would melt at one specific temperature, not over a 6°C range.

options.text: A substance that is natural and unprocessed
A substance that contains only one type of element or compound
A substance that is safe to consume
A substance that has been filtered

questions.explanation: In chemistry, 'pure' means a substance contains only one type of element or compound with no other substances mixed in. This is different from the everyday use of 'pure' (e.g., 'pure orange juice' which is actually a mixture). Pure water contains only H₂O molecules; 'pure' mineral water is actually a mixture of water and dissolved minerals.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of a formulation?

options.text: Pure distilled water
A single crystal of sodium chloride
Paint, which contains pigment, solvent, binder, and additives in specific proportions
A sample of pure iron

questions.explanation: A formulation is a mixture that has been designed with a precise composition for a specific purpose. Paint is a formulation because it contains carefully measured amounts of pigment (colour), solvent (helps it spread), binder (holds it together), and additives (improve properties). Other examples include medicines, cleaning products, and alloys.

questions.stem: Pure water boils at exactly 100°C at standard pressure. A sample of water is tested and boils at 102°C. What can you conclude?

options.text: The water is pure but the pressure is different
The water contains dissolved impurities that raise the boiling point
The thermometer is reading 2°C too high
Both A and B are possible explanations

questions.explanation: Both explanations are possible. Dissolved impurities raise the boiling point above 100°C (this is called boiling point elevation). However, if the atmospheric pressure is higher than standard pressure, even pure water would boil above 100°C. In an exam, if told the pressure is standard, the answer would be impurities. Both factors can affect boiling point.

questions.stem: How does the melting point of a substance help determine its purity?

options.text: Pure substances melt at higher temperatures than mixtures
Pure substances have a sharp melting point; impurities lower it and broaden the range
Mixtures do not melt at all
Pure substances have a broad melting range

questions.explanation: A pure substance melts at a single, sharp temperature (e.g., pure ice melts at exactly 0°C). When impurities are present, the melting point is lowered and the substance melts over a range of temperatures rather than at a fixed point. Comparing the measured melting point to the known value can indicate purity.
